title: ACRES Act
official_title: To require that the Secretary of Agriculture and the Secretary of the Interior submit accurate reports regarding hazardous fuels reduction activities, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors, but the bill cleared the House by voice vote and the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee ordered it reported favorably without amendment — the metadata shows no organized opposition. A transparency mandate with no new spending attached rarely draws floor resistance; the main variable is Senate scheduling.
summary: Makes the Forest Service and Interior Department report honestly on how many acres of federal land they actually treated to reduce wildfire fuel each year — counting each acre only once, even if it was treated multiple times. The reports go to Congress with the President's budget and must be posted publicly.
brief: Requires annual, publicly posted counts of acres treated for wildfire fuel reduction, with each completed acre counted only once and no credit for awarding contracts.

items.main: Names the Act the "Accurately Counting Risk Elimination Solutions Act" or the "ACRES Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Accurate Hazardous Fuels Reduction Reports

items.main: Requires the Agriculture and Interior Secretaries to report each year, in the materials supporting the President's budget, the number of federal acres where hazardous fuels reduction work was completed the prior fiscal year.
items.detail: Only completed activities are recorded, and each acre is counted once regardless of how many treatments it received. Reports must break out which acres sit in the wildland-urban interface, wildfire risk levels (high, moderate, or low) at the start and end of the period, whether work came from a managed wildfire or a planned project, cost per acre, the region or system unit, and the treatments' effectiveness at reducing wildfire risk. Each report must be posted on the departments' websites.

items.main: Orders standardized data-tracking procedures within 90 days of enactment, with a report to Congress due 2 weeks after the procedures are in place.
items.detail: The procedures must include regular accuracy reviews, verification methods tying data to actual work performed, analysis of short- and long-term effectiveness, and methods to distinguish acres inside versus outside the wildland-urban interface. The report to Congress must describe the procedures and recommend fixes for any tracking limitations.

items.main: Directs a GAO study of the Act's implementation within 2 years, and authorizes no additional funds for any of it.
items.detail: "Hazardous fuels reduction activity" is defined as vegetation management that reduces wildfire risk — including mechanical treatments and prescribed burning — and expressly excludes the mere awarding of contracts. The Agriculture Secretary covers National Forest System lands; the Interior Secretary covers public lands and National Park System units.

underreported.summary: Each acre is recorded once per reporting period regardless of how many hazardous fuels reduction activities occurred on it, and only completed activities are recorded.
underreported.why_unreported: The section label promises accurate reports; the operative rule changes the counting method itself, which mechanically produces lower acre totals than counting every treatment on the same land.

underreported.summary: The definition of hazardous fuels reduction activity excludes the awarding of contracts to conduct such activities.
underreported.why_unreported: This bars agencies from counting acres as treated when a contract has been signed but no work completed — a definitional limit not apparent from the bill's title.

gaps: Reports must state the effectiveness of treatments at reducing wildfire risk, but the bill does not define how effectiveness is to be measured.
The bill mandates new tracking procedures, reviews, and reports but authorizes no additional funds to carry them out.
Reports must give wildfire risk levels (high, moderate, or low) at the start and end of each period, but the bill does not say who assigns those levels or by what standard.
The report on tracking limitations must include policy recommendations, but the bill sets no process or deadline for acting on them.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Westerman
featured_quotes.text: This is, I think, a small step in the right direction, and it shouldn't cost any more to report accurate data than to report inaccurate data. I look forward to passing this bill as well as some larger bills like the Fix Our Forests Act that we hope to have before the body this week.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Tiffany
featured_quotes.text: In spite of what was just said on the other side of the aisle, I want to invite the gentleman from California to Wisconsin. He can get some good fishing in in northern Minnesota, good musky fishing, but if the gentleman wants the best, then come to northern Wisconsin. I have an invitation for my friend. This bill will bring transparency, Mr. Speaker, to the misleading and inaccurate way hazardous fuels treatments are reported.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Huffman
featured_quotes.text: I look forward to working with our friends across the aisle on the accounting issue that has been discussed here today. Obviously, we want to make sure that the Forest Service is not taking advance credit for phases of projects that haven't happened yet. I think that is for the most part what has happened that the gentleman from Arkansas identified. I don't believe there has been any actual double or triple counting, but either way, we want it to be accurate. We all need good, accurate data on that reporting. We will work together on that.
